No, not all prime numbers are even. Prime numbers greater than 2 are always odd. This is because any number divisible by 2 (the smallest even number) would be even itself and thus not prime. To verify this, consider that for any prime number \( p \geq 3 \):

1. If \( p = 2 \), it is a prime number.
2. For any odd prime number \( p > 2 \), it cannot be divisible by 2 because the sum of the digits of \( p \) (if all digits are different) will always end in an even number, and thus cannot be 2.

To illustrate this, let's check a few prime numbers:

- The smallest odd prime number is 3. Its digits are all odd, so \( 3 + 3 = 6 \), which ends in an even digit. Therefore, 3 is not prime.
- The next odd prime number is 5. Its digits are all odd, so \( 5 + 5 = 10 \), which ends in an even digit. Therefore, 5 is not prime.
- The next odd prime number is 7. Its digits are all odd, so \( 7 + 7 = 14 \), which ends in an even digit. Therefore, 7 is not prime.

This pattern continues for any odd prime number greater than 2.
